# Adaptive Test-Time Compute Allocation with Evolving In-Context Demonstrations

- **Authors**: Bowen Zuo, Dongruo Zhou, Yinglun Zhu
- **Venue**: ACL
- **Published**: unknown
- **Source**: anthology
- **Link**: <https://aclanthology.org/2026.findings-acl.1754/>
- **PDF**: <https://aclanthology.org/2026.findings-acl.1754.pdf>
- **DOI**: 10.18653/v1/2026.findings-acl.1754
- **Topics**: overthinking
- **Relevance score**: overthinking 0.50

## In one line

A test-time-compute-allocation framework unifies where to spend compute (which unresolved queries get more sampling) with how generation is performed there (conditioning new samples on in-context demonstrations retrieved, via semantic similarity, from other queries already solved during the same inference run) -- consistently beating uniform Best-of-N and a difficulty-adaptive elimination baseline in coverage-per-token across four model families and multiple math/coding/reasoning benchmarks, with gains concentrated early in test-time scaling.

## Problem

Existing test-time-scaling methods share a common limitation: they allocate additional inference-time samples uniformly or based on estimated per-question difficulty, but always keep the underlying per-question sampling distribution fixed and static throughout generation -- so once a question's easy solutions (high probability under the base distribution) are exhausted, further independent sampling from the same unchanged distribution yields diminishing returns on the genuinely hard, low-base-probability cases that remain.

## Contributions

- a unified framework for test-time compute allocation that jointly decides where to spend additional inference compute (which unresolved queries) and how generation there is performed (by reshaping the sampling distribution via evolving in-context demonstrations), rather than treating these as separate concerns as in prior adaptive-allocation work
- a two-stage warm-up-then-adaptive-sampling algorithm that reuses successfully-solved test queries as ICL demonstrations for still-unsolved, semantically related queries, letting the effective generation distribution evolve as more of the test set is resolved during the same inference run
- a controlled experiment isolating that similarity-guided (not merely present) in-context demonstrations drive reliable coverage gains, since randomly-selected demonstrations sometimes underperform simpler non-adaptive baselines on reasoning-heavy tasks
- consistent coverage and token-efficiency improvements over uniform Best-of-N and a difficulty-adaptive elimination baseline across four model families and five math/coding/reasoning benchmarks, with gains concentrated early in the scaling curve, plus demonstrated compatibility with alternative distribution-reshaping mechanisms (temperature adjustment) and non-oracle aggregation (self-consistency)

## Method

Frames adaptive test-time compute allocation as a sequential decision process operating on a test set jointly, evaluated via 'coverage' (whether at least one generated response for a question is correct, per a reward oracle). The method has two stages: (1) Warm-up -- a small, fixed number of responses is generated per question from the base conditional distribution; any question with a response scoring above threshold gamma is marked solved and removed from further consideration, while the remaining unsolved questions and their first correct answers (where found) populate an evolving candidate pool D_test; this both resolves easy queries cheaply and produces an initial set of usable in-context demonstrations. (2) Adaptive Distribution Sampling -- for each still-unresolved query, an ICL prompt is constructed from its P most semantically similar neighbor questions (via embedding cosine similarity) among the ever-growing pool of solved queries, using each neighbor's most recently found correct answer as its demonstration; new responses are then sampled from this ICL-conditioned distribution (not the base distribution), so the effective sampling distribution reshapes itself as more queries get solved and enter the demonstration pool, unifying compute allocation (concentrating rounds on unresolved queries) with distributional adaptation (using solved sibling queries' successful reasoning as guidance) within a single inference-time loop requiring no parameter updates. A controlled pilot experiment on GPQA-Diamond confirms the mechanism's premise: at matched sampling budget, conditioning generation on semantically-neighboring solved-question demonstrations consistently yields higher coverage than a fixed/generic prompt (Table 1: e.g. 8-samples-per-question coverage 85.86% for neighbor-conditioned vs. 83.84% for fixed).

## Results

Across four model families/configurations (Gemini-2.5-flash-lite non-thinking, Gemini-2.5-flash-lite thinking, GPT-4.1 Mini, GPT-5 Nano) and five benchmarks (MATH-500, LiveCodeBench, MinervaMath, GPQA-Diamond, a custom hard-difficulty Reasoning Gym set), the full method (adaptive allocation + similarity-based ICL demonstration evolution) achieves the highest coverage-per-token-budget curve versus three baselines -- Uniform Best-of-N, an Elimination-based adaptive-allocation method (samples concentrated on unresolved queries but still drawn from a fixed distribution), and a random-demonstration ablation of the proposed method itself -- consistently dominating on nearly all benchmark/model combinations, with gains most pronounced under tighter token budgets and emerging early in the scaling curve (indicating more efficient allocation rather than reliance on late-stage oversampling). On LiveCodeBench specifically, the gap over Elimination and Uniform is especially large for the non-thinking Gemini model (coverage rising to ~48% at a fraction of the token budget competing methods need to reach ~35-40%). The random-demonstration variant of the method ('Ours (Rand)') still generally outperforms Uniform and Elimination (confirming adaptive allocation alone, even without similarity-guided demonstrations, already helps), but underperforms the full similarity-based method, and on some reasoning-intensive benchmarks (Reasoning Gym, MinervaMath, LiveCodeBench) random demonstrations occasionally underperform even Uniform or Elimination outright, especially for reasoning-oriented models -- direct evidence that unstructured added context is not reliably beneficial and that similarity-guided demonstration selection specifically, not merely adaptive allocation or added context per se, drives the consistent, stable gains. Token-efficiency analysis (excluding simulated thinking-summary tokens for reasoning models) shows the full method consistently achieves the highest token efficiency of all compared approaches -- reaching a given accuracy level with fewer generated tokens across all benchmarks and models. Ablations: replacing the evolving in-context demonstrations with progressive temperature increase (a simpler, alternative way to reshape the sampling distribution without ICL) also improves over fixed-demonstration or purely uniform baselines, confirming the framework is agnostic to the specific distribution-reshaping mechanism used, though the paper's main reported results use ICL; self-consistency-based aggregation (rather than ground-truth-oracle-based elimination) also shows the method outperforming baselines when using accuracy rather than coverage as the metric, extending applicability to settings without a ground-truth verifier; a controlled noisy-reward experiment (randomly flipping 5% of binary correctness labels used to decide whether a response solves a question and enters the demonstration pool) is introduced to test robustness under imperfect verification, though the paper's summary of this specific result is not fully detailed in the excerpted pages. Compared against a fixed-demonstration variant of the elimination baseline (using standard, static prompt templates from prior work rather than randomly-selected or similarity-selected examples), the dynamic method retains an advantage in both token efficiency and accuracy even when its own demonstration selection is random, underscoring that adaptivity in the generation distribution itself (not just in sample allocation) is what drives the improvement over static-distribution baselines.

## Limitations

The method depends on a reward oracle (or, in the self-consistency variant, a consensus-based proxy) to decide when a query is solved and to select which response becomes a future in-context demonstration; the paper's own robustness check under a 5% noisy-reward-flipping setting suggests some sensitivity to verifier quality is a live concern the authors found worth testing explicitly. Random demonstration selection (an ablation of the proposed method) is shown to sometimes underperform simpler non-adaptive baselines on reasoning-intensive benchmarks specifically for reasoning-oriented models, indicating the full method's gains rely on the similarity-based demonstration-selection component functioning correctly rather than the adaptive-allocation mechanism alone being sufficient. Evaluation is limited to four specific model configurations accessed via public APIs; broader coverage across open-weight models or substantially larger benchmarks is not reported in the excerpted experiments.

## Why it matters here

- **overthinking**: Indirectly relevant to test-time compute efficiency: this targets how additional inference-time compute is allocated *across a test set* and how the sampling distribution for hard queries is reshaped using other queries' already-solved reasoning, rather than the length or productiveness of any single reasoning trace, but it shares this archive's central concern that resampling from an unchanged distribution has diminishing returns and that a genuinely adaptive mechanism (here, in-context conditioning on sibling successes rather than blind resampling) recovers coverage other test-time-scaling methods waste compute chasing.

## Abstract

While scaling test-time compute can substantially improve model performance, existing approaches either rely on static compute allocation or sample from fixed generation distributions.In this work, we introduce a test-time compute allocation framework that jointly adapts where computation is spent and how generation is performed. Our method begins with a warm-up phase that identifies easy queries and assembles an initial pool of question-response pairs from the test set itself. An adaptive phase then concentrates further computation on unresolved queries while reshaping their generation distributions through evolving in-context demonstrations—conditioning each generation on successful responses from semantically related queries rather than resampling from a fixed distribution.Experiments across math, coding, and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms existing baselines while consuming substantially less inference-time compute.
